Prop Edge Engine · NFL 2026 · Week 1

Week 1 Picks

Paper picks, logged before kickoff and scored Monday. The model has not yet shown it can beat the book in Week 1, so every pick here is an argument, not a promise. This is analysis, not advice.

Built Fri Sep 4, 5:51 pm PDT from DraftKings odds captured 2026-09-04 at 10:27 ET. Next update: Friday Sep 11 evening, after the 4 pm ET injury report (Week 1 practice reports start Wed Sep 9). How the picks are made.

How to read this page
The model behind these picks has shown no skill over last year's averages in Week 1 in three seasons of testing. These are paper picks by the engine's own rules: logged before kickoff, scored Monday against results and closing lines. As of 2026-09-03 the engine covers every skill position and market the book lists: passing yards and touchdowns, rushing yards, receiving yards and receptions for backs and tight ends as well as receivers, and same-game combinations priced from one simulation of the offense.

Three views. Picks is the sheet: the legs worth a bet, each with its price, the chance the price implies and the chance the model gives it. Games has one card per game in DraftKings order: kickoff, venue, roof, total, spread, the kickoff forecast, the verdict, the pick and its checks, the book's main lines and the players the model covers. All odds is every ladder the book listed, every rung, beside the model's chance.

Verdicts. Play means we would bet it: our number says it hits more often than the price suggests, the player did it often enough last year to back that up, and the defense he faces does not argue against it. A Play also has to keep at least 10 points of edge in the worst case, meaning if the opposing defense repeats last season in full (the Sensitivity line on each pick). Lean means we like it but something real gets in the way, so we are not betting it and it stays out of parlays; if you bet it anyway, bet small. Pass means the price is fair or too short, so there is no bet.

Parlays. Legs in different games multiply exactly, so the slip price is the product of the leg prices. For legs in the same game DraftKings reprices for correlation, and the displayed price will be lower than the product shown.

Weather. Each card shows the roof and the kickoff-hour forecast: weather.gov when its hourly forecast reaches the kickoff (about 6.5 days out), Open-Meteo before that, each labelled with the source. Rain enters the model as a chance shared by everyone in the game; wind of 15 mph or more shortens the passing game; indoor games carry no weather term.

Players tables. QB is the passer expected to start ("new" marks a change from last season, which the model discounts). Role is the share of the team's pass plays the receiver ran a route on last season, plus expected carries for backs; it is the volume input the model uses. Snap percent is for reference.

The picks

Book says is how often the price says it should hit. Model says is how often we think it hits. When ours is higher, that gap is the whole reason to bet. Odds are DraftKings prices at capture and move.

Every leg carries its reasons as bullets. Singles first, then the same-game pairs that only make sense together.

Lean 1 · single New this build: the yards leg replaces the touchdown leg for Maye. Trailing at Seattle means throwing.
1.1NE Patriots @ SEA SeahawksDrake Maye (NE)250+ passing yards+16138%61%
  • Top five in the league last year in completions, yards and touchdowns, and he threw for 250 or more in 12 of 17 games; the price says it happens fewer than four times in ten.
  • New England traded two premium picks for A.J. Brown, a six-time 1,000-yard receiver, and kept Hunter Henry and Mack Hollins; there are more places for the yards to go, not fewer.
  • Wednesday night opener at Seattle with a 44.5 total and Seattle favored by 3.5: New England is expected to trail, which usually means throwing. That helps this leg and hurts the touchdown one, which is why this is a Play and the 2+ touchdowns is a Lean.
  • Seattle, honestly: last year they allowed 6.03 yards per pass attempt, the fewest in the league (league 7.02), yet they faced 35 throws a game, above average, because teams trailed and kept throwing. That is why a 250-yard passer still got there in 6 of 17 games against them, and in 4 of 8 games in Seattle, right at the league average. Maye himself reached 250 in 2 of 3 games against top-ten pass defenses (273, 282, 155).
  • Home field: league-wide, a visiting offense throws for about 1 to 4 percent fewer yards per attempt than at home depending on the years measured; the engine carries no separate home term for passing because the effect was near zero in the seasons it was tuned on. Seattle's own defense has allowed more per attempt at Lumen Field (6.90) than on the road (6.57) over the last three seasons, and 13 of 26 visiting quarterbacks reached 250 there. Maye on the road: 8 of 14 at 250+.
  • Injury, checked Fri Sep 4 (ESPN; no official Week 1 report until practice reports start Wed Sep 9): Maye not listed. TreVeyon Henderson (NE) questionable, ankle. Wednesday game: final report Tuesday.
  • Why this is a Lean, not a Play (rule tightened Sep 4 evening): a Play now has to keep at least 10 points of edge even if the opposing defense repeats last season in full. Maye keeps 7 (45 against 38) against the league's best pass defense per attempt. Good bet by the numbers, too thin for the sheet's most extreme matchup. It comes back as a Play if the price lengthens past +200 or the practice reports change the New England picture.
  • Opponent, with numbers: SEA allowed 212.88 passing yards a game last year against a league average of 224.68 (12th fewest of 32), 6.03 yards per attempt (7.02 league, 1st fewest of 32) while facing 35.3 attempts a game (32.0 league), and a quarterback reached 250 against them in 6 of 17 games (league average 6.1; 17th fewest of 32). SEA blitzed on 28% of dropbacks (league 30%); blitzing raises sacks and touchdown passes and lowers completions, and the model applies that mix. A real minus for this leg.
  • Worst case: Model 61 in 100 as built. If SEA's defense repeats last season in full, 45. The price says 38. Thinner, still favorable.

Longer parlays across bet types (lottery tickets)

Cross-game slips built from the best-value leg in each game across every market, one leg per game, so the price is exactly the product of the legs. A leg qualifies only if it clears the model's 3-point bar in the 35% to 75% book band, is not a mover, carries no new-quarterback or teammate-absence flag, was not rejected in this week's review, and the player's own record last season at that rung is at least what the price asks. Every added leg multiplies both the payout and the chance of losing; these hit a few times a season at best.

How the picks are made

Each game is simulated thousands of times as one offense: the play count, the split between dropbacks and runs, every receiver's targets, catches and yards, every back's carries and yards, and the quarterback's passing line as the sum of what his receivers do plus the throws to everyone else. A quarterback's passing yards and his receiver's yards are therefore priced together, and a back's carries fall in the same simulated games where the passing volume rises.

Behind that sit every receiver's route share, target rate, depth of target, catch rate and yards per catch, both teams' tempo, the total and spread, venue, kickoff window and forecast. The opposing defense enters as five measured terms (yards per target, catch rate, passing touchdowns per attempt, yards per carry and rushing touchdowns per carry allowed, each relative to the league and shrunk hard because defense barely repeats year to year) plus the total and spread. Teammates share the game's pass volume, so paired legs are priced together. A leg makes the list only when the model's number beats the price by a clear margin, the player's own record supports it, and a plain-language reason survives. Games a teammate missed count at 30%, games under a different quarterback at 50%, deep rungs are excluded, and players on a new team are shown but never picked.

The lean
Drake Maye (NE) 250+ passing yards at +161.
  • Top five in the league last year in completions, yards and touchdowns, and he threw for 250 or more in 12 of 17 games; the price says it happens fewer than four times in ten.
  • New England traded two premium picks for A.J. Brown, a six-time 1,000-yard receiver, and kept Hunter Henry and Mack Hollins; there are more places for the yards to go, not fewer.
  • Wednesday night opener at Seattle with a 44.5 total and Seattle favored by 3.5: New England is expected to trail, which usually means throwing. That helps this leg and hurts the touchdown one, which is why this is a Play and the 2+ touchdowns is a Lean.
  • Seattle, honestly: last year they allowed 6.03 yards per pass attempt, the fewest in the league (league 7.02), yet they faced 35 throws a game, above average, because teams trailed and kept throwing. That is why a 250-yard passer still got there in 6 of 17 games against them, and in 4 of 8 games in Seattle, right at the league average. Maye himself reached 250 in 2 of 3 games against top-ten pass defenses (273, 282, 155).
  • Home field: league-wide, a visiting offense throws for about 1 to 4 percent fewer yards per attempt than at home depending on the years measured; the engine carries no separate home term for passing because the effect was near zero in the seasons it was tuned on. Seattle's own defense has allowed more per attempt at Lumen Field (6.90) than on the road (6.57) over the last three seasons, and 13 of 26 visiting quarterbacks reached 250 there. Maye on the road: 8 of 14 at 250+.
  • Injury, checked Fri Sep 4 (ESPN; no official Week 1 report until practice reports start Wed Sep 9): Maye not listed. TreVeyon Henderson (NE) questionable, ankle. Wednesday game: final report Tuesday.
  • Why this is a Lean, not a Play (rule tightened Sep 4 evening): a Play now has to keep at least 10 points of edge even if the opposing defense repeats last season in full. Maye keeps 7 (45 against 38) against the league's best pass defense per attempt. Good bet by the numbers, too thin for the sheet's most extreme matchup. It comes back as a Play if the price lengthens past +200 or the practice reports change the New England picture.
  • Opponent, with numbers: SEA allowed 212.88 passing yards a game last year against a league average of 224.68 (12th fewest of 32), 6.03 yards per attempt (7.02 league, 1st fewest of 32) while facing 35.3 attempts a game (32.0 league), and a quarterback reached 250 against them in 6 of 17 games (league average 6.1; 17th fewest of 32). SEA blitzed on 28% of dropbacks (league 30%); blitzing raises sacks and touchdown passes and lowers completions, and the model applies that mix. A real minus for this leg.
  • Worst case: Model 61 in 100 as built. If SEA's defense repeats last season in full, 45. The price says 38. Thinner, still favorable.

Matthew Stafford (LA) 2+ passing touchdowns at -155.
  • The reigning MVP threw two or more touchdowns in 15 of 17 games last year, 2.7 a game.

  • The passing game runs through the tight ends and Davante Adams as much as Nacua; the one game Nacua missed, in London, Stafford threw five.
  • Indoors in Melbourne on a Thursday night: no weather, and the model's primetime discount is already applied.
  • Injury, checked Fri Sep 4 (ESPN; no official Week 1 report until practice reports start Wed Sep 9): Not listed. Puka Nacua (LA) is questionable with a groin and was off to the side at practice; the one game Nacua missed last year Stafford threw five touchdowns, so a Nacua absence is not a minus for this leg. Thursday game in Melbourne: the final report comes Wednesday.

The pick
Amon-Ra St. Brown (DET) 9+ receptions at +291.
  • Detroit's WR1 by a mile: 10.1 targets a game, about half the Lions' receiver targets.
  • Nine or more catches in 6 of 17 games last year against a price that says about one in four.
  • A volume catcher, not a deep threat: his catches come on short and intermediate routes that survive good coverage.
  • Injury, checked Fri Sep 4 (ESPN; no official Week 1 report until practice reports start Wed Sep 9): Not listed. Sam LaPorta (DET) is questionable with a hip but has returned to practice; a limited LaPorta would push targets toward St. Brown and Williams.
  • Opponent, with numbers: A receiver reached 9 catches against NO in 0 of 17 games last year (league average 1.8; 1st fewest of 32). NO allowed 7.23 yards per target (7.38 league, 14th fewest of 32) and a 67.5% catch rate (67.5% league). NO blitzed on 34% of dropbacks (league 30%); blitzing raises sacks and touchdown passes and lowers completions, and the model applies that mix. A real minus for this leg.
  • Worst case: Model 30 in 100 as built. If NO's defense repeats last season in full, 30. The price says 26. Barely favorable in the worst case.

Verdict
LeanJakobi Meyers (JAX) 5+ receptions at +179. The model is ahead of the price but the football case has a hole; see the reasons below.
The lean
Jakobi Meyers (JAX) 5+ receptions at +179.
  • A full-time starter priced as a fourth option: he ran about nine of every ten Jacksonville routes after the trade.
  • Caught five or more in 7 of 16 games last season across Las Vegas and Jacksonville; the price says about one in three.
  • The year before he was the Raiders' WR1 at 8.6 targets a game. The role, not the name, is what the book is underpricing.
  • Injury, checked Fri Sep 4 (no official Week 1 report exists yet; practice reports start Wed Sep 9, final report Fri Sep 11 at 4 pm ET): Meyers hurt his right wrist in the second week of the preseason, wore a cast, and did not play in any of the three preseason games. Coach Liam Coen, a few days after the roster cutdown: "Jakobi should be going today, went yesterday. He was just limited in terms of catching it a little bit." ESPN listed him questionable (hand) on Sep 2.
  • Why this is a Lean for now: a receptions bet lives on the hands, and the newest word is a catching limitation after a month in a cast. The numbers say Play (edge 8 to 9 points, 7 of 16). It goes back to Play if he is a full participant Wednesday through Friday next week with no designation; it comes off the sheet if he is limited or questionable on Friday.
  • Opponent, with numbers: A receiver reached 5 catches against CLE in 8 of 17 games last year (league average 10.8; 2nd fewest of 32). CLE allowed 6.92 yards per target (7.38 league, 9th fewest of 32) and a 66.3% catch rate (67.5% league). CLE blitzed on 31% of dropbacks (league 30%); blitzing raises sacks and touchdown passes and lowers completions, and the model applies that mix. A real minus for this leg.
  • Worst case: Model 44 in 100 as built. If CLE's defense repeats last season in full, 45. The price says 36. Holds in the worst case.

Verdict
LeanJaylen Warren (PIT) 50+ rushing yards at +142. The model is ahead of the price but the football case has a hole; see the reasons below.
The lean
Jaylen Warren (PIT) 50+ rushing yards at +142.
  • Pittsburgh lists Warren as the starting back on its first depth chart, and he cleared 50 rushing yards in 9 of 16 games last year; the price says four in ten.
  • Against: the new staff (Mike McCarthy) has said it wants a balanced backfield, and Rico Dowdle, a free-agent addition coming off a big 2025, is listed second. A near-even split makes 50 yards a coin flip, not the model's 57.
  • The surest version of this bet, 30+ rushing yards at -274, is on the achievable sheet: he cleared that in 15 of 16 games.
  • Opponent, with numbers: ATL allowed 4.68 yards per carry last year against a league average of 4.38 (8th most of 32), 125 rushing yards a game against 116, and the opposing lead back reached 50 yards in 12 of 17 games (league average 11.4; 13th most of 32). A plus for this leg.
  • Worst case: Model 57 in 100 as built. If ATL's defense repeats last season in full, 59. The price says 41. Holds in the worst case.

Verdict
LeanJosh Allen (BUF) 250+ passing yards at +179. The model is ahead of the price but the football case has a hole; see the reasons below.
The lean
Josh Allen (BUF) 250+ passing yards at +179.
  • 250 or more in 8 of 16 games last year against a price that says 36 in 100; the model has 48.
  • Against: Houston allowed a 250-yard passer in only 2 of 17 games last year, the second fewest in the league, and Khalil Shakir and Keon Coleman are both questionable. That is a real hole. Lean.
  • Opponent, with numbers: HOU allowed 204.12 passing yards a game last year against a league average of 224.68 (6th fewest of 32), 6.47 yards per attempt (7.02 league, 7th fewest of 32) while facing 31.5 attempts a game (32.0 league), and a quarterback reached 250 against them in 2 of 17 games (league average 6.1; 1st fewest of 32). HOU blitzed on 25% of dropbacks (league 30%); blitzing raises sacks and touchdown passes and lowers completions, and the model applies that mix. A real minus for this leg.
  • Worst case: Model 48 in 100 as built. If HOU's defense repeats last season in full, 36. The price says 36. Edge gone if the defense repeats.

PlayTony Pollard (TEN) 60+ rushing yards at +114.
The pick
Tony Pollard (TEN) 60+ rushing yards at +114.
  • Tennessee's starting back, and the staff has said so through camp. Tyjae Spears takes passing downs; Pollard takes early downs and the goal line.
  • Cleared 60 rushing yards in 9 of 17 games last year against a price that says four in nine.
  • Home against the Jets in the lowest total on the slate (38.5), the kind of game that stays on the ground.
  • Injury, checked Fri Sep 4 (ESPN; no official Week 1 report until practice reports start Wed Sep 9): Not listed. Backfield partner Tyjae Spears (TEN) not listed. On the Jets' side Breece Hall (NYJ) is expected ready, which does not touch this leg.
  • Opponent, with numbers: NYJ allowed 4.43 yards per carry last year against a league average of 4.38 (9th most of 32), 136 rushing yards a game against 116, and the opposing lead back reached 60 yards in 13 of 17 games (league average 9.5; 2nd most of 32). A plus for this leg.
  • Worst case: Model 57 in 100 as built. If NYJ's defense repeats last season in full, 57. The price says 47. Holds in the worst case.
